title: Evaluation, Testing & Observability
summary: "I tried a few prompts and it looked good" isn't evaluation, it's a vibe check on a handful of lucky examples. Every system this course has built needs a systematic way to measure whether it's actually working, and whether a change made it better or worse.
objectives: Explain why an ad hoc "looks good" check doesn't substitute for a systematic eval
Design labeled eval test cases with an explicit, checkable criterion each
Explain the tradeoffs of LLM-as-judge scoring versus deterministic, rule-based checks
Implement an eval harness that scores outputs against test cases and flags regressions against a baseline

lessons.title: "It looked fine" is not an evaluation
Interactive: spot the usable eval test case
LLM-as-judge: useful, but not free of the problem it's solving
Prefer deterministic checks wherever they apply
Build it: a deterministic eval harness
Before the checkpoint: what you should now be able to do

exercise.label: Code exercise · Python, runs in a real sandboxed Python interpreter (Pyodide)
exercise.instructions: Complete `evaluate_model(test_cases, model_fn, baseline_score)`. `test_cases` is a list of `{"id":..., "input":..., "check":...}` dicts, where `check(actual)` returns True/False. For each case, call `model_fn(input)` to get the actual output (never let a raise from `model_fn` OR `check` crash your function, treat either as a failed case instead), then run `check(actual)`. Return `{"score":..., "passCount":..., "total":..., "results":..., "regression":...}`, where `results` is a list of `{"id":..., "pass":..., "actual":...}` in the same order as `test_cases`, `score` is `passCount / total`, and `regression` is `True` only when `baseline_score` is a real number AND `score` is lower than it.

hints.title: Hint 1 — conceptual
hints.mdx: Loop over test\_cases: for each one, get an actual output, check it, and record the result. Then reduce that list of results down to a score, a pass count, and a regression flag.

hints.title: Hint 2 — specific
hints.mdx: Wrap the model\_fn(tc\["input"\]) call in its own try/except, if it raises, that case is a fail with actual set to something describing the error, and check() is never called for that case. Separately, wrap tc\["check"\](actual) in try/except too, if IT raises, treat the case as a fail as well.

hints.title: Hint 3 — near-solution
hints.mdx: After building the results list, total is len(results), passCount is how many have pass is True, score is passCount / total (guard against total being 0). regression is only True if baseline\_score is not None AND score \< baseline\_score.

tests.name: All test cases pass: score is 1, regression is false with no baseline provided
tests.hint: Call model_fn(tc['input']) then tc['check'](actual) for each case. score should be passCount/total. With no baseline_score, regression must be False, not None-but-truthy.

tests.name: Mixed pass/fail: score reflects the true pass rate, and results correctly flag exactly which cases failed
tests.hint: Each entry in results should have pass set individually per test case, based on that case's own check(actual) call, not a single shared pass/fail value.

tests.name: A model_fn that raises for one case is caught and counted as a failure, without crashing the other cases
tests.hint: Wrap the model_fn(tc['input']) call in its own try/except. If it raises, that specific case is a fail, but keep processing the remaining test cases normally.

tests.name: regression is true when score is below the baseline, and false when it meets or exceeds it
tests.hint: regression should be (baseline_score is not None) AND (score < baseline_score). A score equal to or above the baseline is NOT a regression.

tests.name: A check() function that raises is treated as a failing check, not a crash of the whole evaluation
tests.hint: Wrap tc['check'](actual) in its own try/except too, separate from the model_fn try/except. If check() raises, that case is a fail, but every other case should still be evaluated normally.

questions.question: Why doesn't "I read a few outputs and they looked fine" substitute for a systematic eval?

options.text: It's an unrepresentative sample judged by inconsistent, undocumented criteria, with no way to compare versions objectively
options.why: A few spot-checked examples, judged by feel, give neither coverage nor a repeatable number to compare against later.

options.text: It's fine for small projects, systematic eval is only needed once a system reaches production scale
options.why: The problem isn't scale, it's rigor, a small project with no systematic eval still can't reliably tell whether a change helped or hurt, it just has fewer users affected by not knowing.

options.text: It doesn't substitute for eval only when the outputs are structured (JSON), free-text outputs are fine to spot-check
options.why: The reasoning applies regardless of output format, structured or free-text, an unrepresentative sample judged inconsistently doesn't produce a trustworthy, comparable signal either way.

questions.principle: A few spot-checked examples, judged by feel, give neither coverage nor a repeatable number to compare against later.

questions.question: What specific risk does LLM-as-judge scoring introduce that a deterministic exact-match check doesn't have?

options.text: The judge's own grading is itself an unverified model output, it can be inconsistent or biased, unlike a fixed-logic check that behaves identically every time
options.why: LLM-as-judge inherits the exact unreliability it's being used to measure, since the judge is itself a model call.

options.text: LLM-as-judge is always slower, that's its only real downside compared to deterministic checks
options.why: Speed and cost are real downsides, but not the core risk this module highlights, the deeper issue is that the judge's scoring itself isn't guaranteed consistent or correct.

options.text: There's no meaningful difference, both approaches carry identical reliability risk
options.why: There is a meaningful difference, a deterministic check (exact match, schema validation) produces the exact same result every time on the same input, an LLM judge is not guaranteed to.

questions.principle: LLM-as-judge inherits the exact unreliability it's being used to measure, since the judge is itself a model call.

questions.question: When a task's correctness CAN be checked with fixed logic (schema validation, exact match, a numeric comparison), which approach should be preferred?

options.text: The deterministic check, it's consistent, cheap, and exactly reproducible
options.why: Wherever a fixed correct answer or shape exists, a deterministic check is strictly more trustworthy and cheaper than an LLM-as-judge call.

options.text: LLM-as-judge, it generalizes better even to cases with a known correct answer
options.why: When a fixed correct answer or shape already exists, there's nothing for an LLM judge to 'generalize' that a deterministic check doesn't already handle exactly and consistently.

options.text: Whichever is cheaper to run for this specific test case
options.why: Cost isn't the deciding factor here, deterministic checks are both cheaper AND more reliable when they apply, there's no tradeoff to weigh in that scenario.

questions.principle: Wherever a fixed correct answer or shape exists, a deterministic check is strictly more trustworthy and cheaper than an LLM-as-judge call.

questions.question: An eval run passes 7 of 10 test cases. The recorded baseline score is 0.75. Using this module's definition, is this a regression? (Enter 1 for yes, 0 for no.)

numeric.correct: Correct. 7/10 = 0.70, which is below the 0.75 baseline, so this is a regression.
numeric.incorrect: Not quite. 7/10 = 0.70, which is LOWER than the 0.75 baseline, so this does count as a regression (answer: 1).

questions.question: A team changes their system prompt (Module 1) and their retrieval top-k (Module 3) in the same deploy, then runs the eval suite once and sees a score drop. What's the practical downside of evaluating both changes together instead of separately?

options.text: They can't tell which change caused the drop, or whether one change improved things while the other hurt worse, isolating the cause now requires re-running the eval with each change separated
options.why: Evaluating both changes together conflates their effects, the score drop is real, but its cause is ambiguous until the changes are isolated and re-tested separately.

options.text: Nothing, the eval score is the same either way regardless of how many things changed at once
options.why: The score reflects the combined effect of both changes together, it can't distinguish which one, or how much of each, is responsible for the drop.

options.text: The eval suite itself becomes invalid once more than one variable changes between runs
options.why: The eval suite still produces a valid, meaningful score, the problem isn't the eval's validity, it's that the CAUSE of a score change becomes ambiguous when multiple variables change at once.

questions.principle: Evaluating both changes together conflates their effects, the score drop is real, but its cause is ambiguous until the changes are isolated and re-tested separately.

glossary.definition: a systematic, repeatable process for scoring outputs against test cases with defined criteria.
a pass/fail criterion evaluated by fixed logic, producing identical results on identical input every time.
using a model call to score another model's output, useful for subjective criteria, but inherits model unreliability.
a previously recorded eval score used as the comparison point for detecting regressions.
a measurable drop in eval score after a change, compared to the baseline.
